item.title: Fidelity Synopses: Pre-Execution Plan Selection for Approximate Vector Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.41407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vector search has become a database operator with many physical implementations: different index families, build-time and search-time parameters, and compressed or disk-resident variants. Each trades cost against fidelity, the fraction of a query's exact top-k nearest neighbors that a configuration returns. Deployments nevertheless choose one configuration offline and use it for every query, so they are sized for their hardest queries and overpay for the rest. On a 5.8M-item LAION benchmark with four embedding models, running each query on the cheapest configuration that suffices for it would roughly halve the cost in a typical setting. Exploiting this requires predicting each configuration's fidelity before running it, which is hard because fidelity is defined by the very exact search that approximate indexes avoid. Relational optimizers solve the analogous problem for cardinality with offline synopses; we propose one for vector search. A fidelity synopsis divides the embedding space into cells around a set of landmarks and records, for every cell and configuration, how often that configuration met a fidelity target on a sample of queries. At query time, one nearest-landmark lookup yields a calibrated estimate for every configuration, and an optimizer chooses configurations so that the workload misses the target no more often than its requirement allows. We test the two premises the synopsis relies on, that fidelity varies smoothly across the embedding space and that its loss is specific to each configuration. Held to the same requirement a static deployment is built to meet, synopsis-guided selection lowers cost in all 16 combinations of model and query direction, to a median of 0.72x the static deployment, with a batched lookup of 21-32 microseconds per query. The saving persists against the best static choice among the same indexes, and within a single index at no extra memory.
item.dc:creator: Adithya Ramanatha, Sanskar S. Singh, Maya Ramanath

item.title: Supervised and LLM-Augmented Cardinality Estimation for Similarity Queries on Knowledge Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.41669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past decades, query cardinality estimation on relational databases has been proven crucial, enabling the result size estimation of all sub-plans of each query. This allowed query optimizers to design efficient query plans, towards minimizing the query response time. Lately, knowledge graphs are being preferred over traditional databases in various applications, due to their ability to represent complex relationships and semantic meaning in a domain-specific context. In this work, we present a novel approach for supervised similarity-aware cardinality estimation on knowledge graphs that incorporates similarities into the model training process, thus treating them as first-class citizens. To this end, we present SCE-KG, a model that employs a novel encoding scheme for cardinality estimation, named SGsplit. We further extend our approach by leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate training queries that resemble realistic user workloads, and show that combining LLM-generated and random walk samples consistently improves estimation accuracy on test workloads generated by two independent LLMs. Our experimental evaluation reveals that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques in terms of prediction error, achieving 40x and 37x improvement for star and chain queries, respectively (95th percentile), whereas its online overhead accounts for less than 0.05% of the average query execution time and less than 1% of the average query planning time, showing a sub-millisecond latency in all cases.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Chatzigeorgakidis, Dimitrios Skoutas, Alkis Simitsis

item.title: CypherGuard: Database-Grounded Correction for Reliable Text-to-Cypher
item.description: arXiv:2610.41755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-Cypher translates natural-language questions into Cypher queries over property graphs. Graph database systems increasingly adopt this translation as a native query interface. Large language models generate fluent Cypher but stay unreliable. On Cypher-Bench a small model answers only 31.4% of questions correctly, and even a strong model plateaus at 71.76%. The dominant failure modes are structural rather than linguistic. For example, a generated query may parse correctly and follow the schema, yet still return zero rows because it traverses a relationship against the stored graph direction. To address this issue, we present CypherGuard, a training-free framework that detects and corrects these structural faults. Our approach uses two core components: a graph-native error taxonomy to guide repair, and a mined rule library to guide query generation. At inference time, CypherGuard first rewrites schema-detectable faults, then re-executes each draft and repairs it only when the query errors or returns nothing. On CypherBench test questions, across seven graphs, CypherGuard reaches 88.50% overall execution accuracy, +25.08% over the same-backbone zero-shot floor, surpassing an RL-fine-tuned 7B specialist and the strongest training-based system that we compare against.
item.dc:creator: Zebin Chen, Dong Wen, Makbule Gulcin Ozsoy, Wenjie Zhang

item.title: Merging and Evolution of Data Bases: A Many-Logic Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.40812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A new approach to information-based logics using many-logic modal structures (MLMSs) was recently proposed by Martins et al. In such a setting, it is possible to have worlds with different underlying logics within the same frame, all anchored to a base lattice that contains the semantics of each logic as a down-complete sublattice. In this paper, we take the lattice L6, defined by the six-valued semantics of the logic of evidence and truth LET + K , as our base lattice. We also consider four-, three-, and two-valued formal systems associated with down-complete sublattices of L6. These logics are capable of representing paracomplete, paraconsistent, and classical contexts with six, four, three, and two informational scenarios, respectively. As applications of MLMSs, we will discuss the merging and temporal evolution of databases whose underlying logics are two-, three-, four-, and six-valued. We will also investigate inconsistency measures in this context.
item.dc:creator: Manuel A. Martins (CIDMA,Dep. of Mathematics), Abilio Rodrigues (Federal University of Minas Gerais)

item.title: A Multimodal Type 2 Diabetes Registry on DHIS2: A Design and Feasibility Study with the AI-READI Dataset
item.description: arXiv:2610.41918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Care for type 2 diabetes increasingly draws on continuous glucose monitors, wearable devices, home sensors, clinical records and retinal images, yet few open platforms have been shown to hold all of these for the same person. We asked three questions of DHIS2, the open-source health information system that ministries of health in about 80 countries run nationally: whether an unmodified Tracker program can represent these modalities together (RQ1), which design choices its row-per-event data model forces for dense sensor streams (RQ2), and what a bulk loader must do to load such data correctly (RQ3). We designed a registry of 27 program stages and 445 data elements, loaded the AI-READI dataset of 2,280 participants into it, and verified the result field by field against the source files. The program held every loaded modality in 8.09 million events. Dense streams were stored as hourly summaries aligned across modalities; electrocardiograms, diagnoses and 118,480 retinal images were stored as one event per record. The event model ruled out storing raw readings, and hourly summaries reduced the wearable and glucose volume about 26-fold. An audit of the loader found defects that shared one pattern: a failure that looked like success. We state five lessons for DHIS2 Tracker clients that address this pattern. Verification of all 64.9 million stored values found four defects, all missing, duplicated or artifactual records rather than wrong values, and none after their repair; an independent recomputation of the glucose summaries agreed on all 464,210 values compared. The paper offers implementation guidance for DHIS2 implementers and for users of AI-READI; it does not evaluate clinical use. Analytics at this scale, use by clinicians and live device feeds remain to be shown.
item.dc:creator: Saptarshi Purkayastha, Aiswarya Nandan Perumbilly, Zhenan Yin, Sherri L. Bucher

item.title: Open Biomedical Knowledge Graphs at Scale: Construction, Federation, and AI Agent Access with Samyama Graph Database
item.description: arXiv:2603.15080v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Biomedical knowledge is fragmented across siloed databases---Reactome, STRING, Gene Ontology, ClinicalTrials.gov, DrugBank, DGIdb, SIDER, PubMed, ClinVar, ChEMBL, OpenTargets, and more. We present an open, reproducible biomedical knowledge graph ecosystem built on Samyama, a Rust-native graph database: three foundational graphs detailed end-to-end---Pathways KG (118,686 nodes, 834,785 edges), Clinical Trials KG (7,774,446 nodes, 26,973,997 edges), and Drug Interactions KG (32,726 nodes, 191,970 edges)---and their expansion into a 22-graph, 2-cohort merged biomedical store (328,130,739 nodes and 1,441,425,733 imported edges, including 295,000 synthetic OMOP CDM patients from Synthea). First, we describe a reproducible ETL and portable .sgsnap snapshot pattern where graphs load alone or compose into one store. Second, we analyze single-store cross-KG integration via query-time property joins and load-time identifier deduplication (--dedup-keys): across all 24 snapshots (Samyama-Graph v1.13.0), 328.1M nodes and 1.44B edges load in 2,269.1 s (37m 49s) within 366.5 GB peak RSS (254 B/edge), merging 132,511 cross-source entities across five audited keys (mondo_id,uniprot_id,go_id,drugbank_id,symbol)---87.8% of the 150,965 Bound A sound-identifier ceiling, with zero conflicting-ID refusals. On a frozen 81-query suite, 62 queries return results (17 data-gap empties, 2 timeouts); on an expanded 200-query oracle suite, 195 of 200 pass (97.5%). Third, we introduce schema-driven Model Context Protocol (MCP) server generation: on the 40-question BiomedQA benchmark over the 3-KG subset, domain-specific MCP tools achieve 98% accuracy vs. 85% for schema-aware text-to-Cypher and 75% for standalone GPT-4o, with zero schema errors.
item.dc:creator: Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru

item.title: Recommendation Systems for Exploratory Data Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2609.39412v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exploratory Data Tasks (EDTs) involve iteratively steering workflows as users refine their subjective goals based on newly emerging insights. EDTs are performed by millions of users with varying levels of expertise to understand unfamiliar data, discover trends, and identify evidence that informs critical decision-making. However, a key challenge in EDTs is the enormous space of possible actions that one can take at each step: users struggle to choose among thousands of joins, transformations, and aggregations, leading to exploration paralysis. Because EDT workflows are interconnected, each choice shapes subsequent exploration, and suboptimal choices can lead to inefficiency, missed insights, confirmation bias, and incomplete coverage. This calls for intelligent recommendations that efficiently guide users toward optimal EDT actions. We envision recommendation as a core capability of data systems, proactively guiding users toward promising actions that lower the barrier to EDTs. This capability becomes even more critical as AI agents emerge as a new class of users that perform EDTs on behalf of humans. EDT recommendation is challenging because the action space is combinatorial and actions are data-dependent, which require costly materialization. Moreover, recommendation often involves bundles or sequences of actions across interdependent tasks, requiring coordination across tasks. In this paper, we present our vision of EDT recommendation systems along two axes: single-task vs. multi-task settings and single-action vs. multi-action recommendations. We outline a research agenda that progresses from recommending individual EDT actions to constrained bundles and sequences of actions, and ultimately to coordinated recommendations across interconnected EDTs. We identify research directions for incorporating various contexts, addressing efficiency challenges, and coordinating across tasks.
item.dc:creator: Anna Fariha, Whanhee Cho

item.title: Tessera: Fast Join-Aggregates over Skewed Sparse Relations in Database Engines
item.description: arXiv:2610.40620v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Join-aggregate queries count or sum matching rows for each pair of values, often over skewed sparse relations in which a few values are frequent and most pairs of values never co-occur. Conventional execution plans materialize billions of intermediate join rows, taking minutes to tens of minutes per query. Recent matrix-based solutions reformulate these queries as matrix multiplication to reduce or avoid this materialization. However, they remain slow because they either store result cells for non-matching pairs or still materialize intermediate join rows for infrequent values. We present Tessera, a skew-aware join-aggregate operator for database engines that avoids both sources of overhead. Specifically, Tessera computes a sparse matrix product directly over the engine's rows, emits only nonzero cells as result rows, and prunes values that cannot meet the query's threshold before multiplication begins. It also offloads the dense block formed by pairs of the most frequent values to a CPU matrix accelerator when that block is dense enough. Experimental results show that Tessera is faster than the fastest existing system by 2.8x to 18.8x. In addition, Tessera outperforms DuckDB's execution plans by up to 1,802x.
item.dc:creator: Gyuyeong Kim

item.title: Towards Universal Tabular Embeddings: A Benchmark Across Data Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2604.21696v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models aim to learn universal representations of tabular data that transfer across tasks and domains, enabling applications such as table retrieval, semantic search and table-based prediction. Despite the growing number of such models, it remains unclear which approach works best in practice, as existing methods are often evaluated under task-specific settings that make direct comparison difficult. To address this, we introduce TEmBed, the Tabular Embedding Test Bed, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating tabular embeddings across four representation levels: cell, row, column, and table. Evaluating a diverse set of tabular representation learning models, we show that which model to use depends on the task and representation level. Our results offer practical guidance for selecting tabular embeddings in real-world applications and lay the groundwork for developing more general-purpose tabular representation models.
item.dc:creator: Liane Vogel, Kavitha Srinivas, Niharika D'Souza, Sola Shirai, Oktie Hassanzadeh, Horst Samulowitz

item.title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2610.22731v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.
item.dc:creator: RuiLong Jiang, Dustin Rhodes, Danny McCormick, Yuta Labur, Reza Rokni
